newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Public relations industry enjoys global boom.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Public relations industry enjoys global boom.

text.p: Companies grappling with fierce competition, demanding consumers and tired workers are increasingly hiring trained "communicators".

Burson-Marsteller, the world's biggest public relations firm, says changes in the way companies do business and an urgent need to spread the corporate message has fuelled a boom in the global public relations industry.
"It (public relations) is coming of age," Alison Canning, chief executive of Burson-Marsteller UK, told Reuters.
"Now more than ever before companies are understanding that communications is not just a "nice to have'. It's a core part of corporate strategy."
Britain's "Marketing" magazine reported recently that turnover at several public relations firms had shot up by 40 percent in the last year.
"The good times are back for the public relations industry," the weekly said.
Public relations agencies are not only getting more and more business from companies, but are also being hired increasingly by political parties and governments.

British opposition politicians were horrified -- but PR people were thrilled -- when Queen Elizabeth said recently she would make Peter Gummer, head of Shandwick public relations agency, and Maurice Saatchi, the advertising guru, life peers.
Gummer and Saatchi have both advised Prime Minister John Major and his Conservative Party.
Canning said another growing area for business was from emerging economies that needed Western investment.
"A lot of Asian, eastern European and Latin American countries are hiring public relations agencies. They need to be visible in major capital markets," she said.
Burson-Marsteller has published a 118-page report on global institutional investor sentiment towards emerging markets.
Public relations agencies are also being hired to sort out companies' "internal communications".

Big corporations are realising they have to do more to motivate employees who are bewildered by new technology and demands, and frightened by buzzwords like "downsizing", "rightsizing" and "outsourcing".

One way to boost staff morale and motivation is to tell employees what's happening in the company, so experts are being hired to set up corporate "intranets" and other internal communications systems.
"There is a growing recognition that good people are few and far between. Your employees are either your assets or liabilities," Canning said.
She said Burson-Marsteller and other big public relations groups, while pleased by growing business, were having to retool themselves to deal with competition from management consultancies.
She said that prompted Burson-Marsteller, which is based in New York, to start a big restructuring programme in the United States in January.

Under the programme, which starts in Europe in October 1996 and Asia in January 1997, geographic divisions are being replaced by global specialised practices, such as corporate, consumer, internal communications, hi-tech and public affairs.
Canning, who announced in July that she would leave Burson-Marsteller in October, says she is going because the restructuring basically wiped out her job function.
But she's upbeat about the public relations industry and expects it to grow rapidly over the next few years.
"It's on an upswing for quite a while. One day we'll get our golden age," she said. "I think it's right around the corner."
